text: To converge is to come together toward the same point from different directions — like three hallways all meeting at the cafeteria. Here, several separate forces — concert money, Super Bowl rules, TV deals — are converging at once, and together they push every new stadium toward a roof.

A paradox is a situation that seems to contradict itself but turns out to be true. Here: taxpayers pay a smaller SHARE of each stadium than they used to — yet more actual dollars than ever, because stadiums cost so much more. A smaller slice of a much bigger pie can still be more pie.
A trade-off is what you give up to get something else — every big choice has one. A roof gets you comfort and year-round concerts; the trade-off is losing real weather and open sky.

A bunker is a sealed concrete shelter built to survive bombs — dark, windowless, cut off from the world. Old domed stadiums felt like sitting inside one, which is why people hated them. The new see-through roofs are the fix for that feeling.
A critique is a careful judgment of what’s wrong (and right) with something. The “concrete bunker” complaint was the original critique of domed stadiums — and the expert says it no longer applies.
An enclosure is anything that closes a space in — here, the roof and walls that seal a stadium off from the sky. An “enclosed venue” just means a roofed-over one.
Here “accounts for” means “makes up” — open-air stadiums account for half the league means half of all NFL stadiums are open-air. Nothing to do with bank accounts.
A super-strong, super-light clear plastic used for modern stadium roofs. Unlike the old concrete domes, an ETFE roof lets daylight pour through — you’re indoors, but it doesn’t feel like a basement.

SoFi Stadium in Los Angeles — one of the newest and most expensive NFL stadiums, with a clear ETFE roof. It’s unusual because private money paid for all of it, zero taxpayer dollars — which is why it “skews the numbers” later in the article.
The seating bowl is the giant bowl-shaped ring of seats wrapped around the field. A partial roof covers the bowl — where the fans sit — while the field itself stays open to the sky.

“The elements” is an old-fashioned way of saying the weather — wind, rain, snow, sun. Keeping “some connection to the elements” means fans still feel a little real outdoors. Not chemistry-class elements.

A retractable roof can open and close, like a giant convertible car. Sounds perfect — but they’re expensive, they break down, and teams end up keeping them closed anyway, so almost nobody builds them anymore.
Virtually means “almost” or “practically” — “virtually no one” means almost nobody at all. It has nothing to do with virtual reality.
A venue is a place where events are held — a stadium, arena, or concert hall. The word choice matters: with a roof, the building stops being just a football field and becomes an all-year event venue.

Conventions are giant organized gatherings — thousands of people meeting up about business, comics, games, anything. They rent huge indoor spaces, which is exactly the kind of money a domed stadium can collect on non-football days.

Not the math class! Here “calculus” means the whole set of pluses and minuses behind a decision. Adding a roof “changes the whole calculus”: suddenly the building can earn money 365 days a year, so the expensive roof starts to make sense.

To rule something out is to eliminate it as a possibility. The NFL requires a roof anywhere the average game-day temperature is below 50 degrees — which rules out most of the country in winter. Want a Super Bowl? Build a roof.
An overwhelming majority means nearly all of it — so much that everything else barely counts. Nearly all of the NFL’s money comes from TV, not from tickets at the gate.
Revenue is the money coming in — everything a business earns before paying its costs. For the NFL, the biggest river of revenue by far is television.
To broadcast is to send a show out over TV, radio, or streaming. Broadcast contracts are the giant deals networks sign for the right to show NFL games — the league’s main source of money.
A slot here is a reserved spot in the TV schedule — like the Monday-night slot. Networks pay fortunes for those time slots, so they hate the thought of weather wrecking one. Not a coin slot.
Called off means canceled. For a network that paid millions to show a game, “called off” is the scariest phrase in the language.

A baseline is the starting point you measure from. A new stadium “runs $2 to $3 billion as a baseline” means that’s the minimum — before extras like a roof add hundreds of millions more. Not the line on a basketball court.

A subsidy is money the government chips in to help pay for something. A “public subsidy” for a stadium means taxpayers cover part of the bill for a billionaire owner’s building — which is exactly why people argue about it.
To strip out a number is to remove it from your math to get a clearer picture. SoFi was 100% privately paid, which drags the average down; strip it out, and the taxpayers’ usual share looks bigger.
Financed means paid for — usually with money arranged or borrowed up front. “Privately financed” means the owners’ own money, not taxpayers’.
To skew numbers is to tilt or distort them so they give a misleading picture. One unusual stadium (SoFi, with zero public money) skews the league-wide average for everyone.

The tab is the bill — like a restaurant check. “Paying less of the tab” means covering a smaller share of the total cost. The catch: a smaller share of a $3 billion tab is still way more money than before.

Below-market means cheaper than what things normally sell for. When a city sells a team land at below-market prices, that’s a hidden gift — real money the public gives up, without it ever showing on a bill.

A tax abatement is an official discount on taxes — the government agrees to charge a company less than the normal amount. It’s another quiet way cities help pay for stadiums without writing a visible check.

Infrastructure is the basic built stuff everything else runs on: roads, ramps, pipes, power lines. Cities often build the highway ramps to the stadium at public expense — another hidden piece of the price.
Sanitation services means trash pickup and sewer service. Even garbage collection can be written into a stadium deal — the city does it free, and the public quietly pays.
A mixed-use area combines homes, shops, offices, and restaurants in one development instead of just one thing. Stadium deals often include a whole mixed-use neighborhood built around the building.
Pledged means promised ahead of time. When decades of future tax money are pledged to pay off stadium debt, the city is spending money it hasn’t even collected yet.

A bond is basically an IOU: the city borrows money from investors and promises to pay it back, with interest, over many years. Stadium bonds are how cities afford billion-dollar buildings — by pushing the cost into the future. Not James Bond, and not glue.
To factor something in is to include it in your math. A stadium deal that looks 50-50 can really be 70-30 against the public — once you factor in the cheap land and all the hidden extras.
A balance sheet is the official list of what’s being paid and owed. “Off-balance-sheet” costs are kept off that official list — real costs, just invisible in the numbers voters are shown.

Economists’ word for spending that just moves around instead of growing. The $300 a family spends at the game is $300 they now DON’T spend at the local restaurant or bowling alley — the money changed places, but the town didn’t get richer. It’s the article’s key idea. (Not a substitute teacher.)

Money “leaks out” of a city’s economy when it’s earned there but spent or saved somewhere else — like water dripping out of a bucket. Stadium money flows to owners and players who live elsewhere, so it drips right out of town.

Debt service means the regular payments on borrowed money — not customer service. To “service that debt” is to keep up those payments. If the stadium doesn’t earn enough to cover them, the city — or the fans — must.
To exceed is to go over or be bigger than. If the city’s debt payments exceed what the stadium brings in, the city loses money year after year.
Fiscal means having to do with government money — taxes, budgets, spending. A “fiscal hole” is a gap in the city’s budget that has to be filled by cutting services or raising taxes.

Taking weather “out of the equation” means removing it as a factor that affects the result — as if you deleted one variable from a math problem. There’s no literal equation; it’s a way of saying weather stops mattering.

Here minimize means to talk about something as if it’s smaller than it really is — to downplay it. The expert says losing weather is a genuine loss and he won’t pretend otherwise. (Not shrinking a window on a screen.)

The 1967 NFL championship game in Green Bay, played in roughly minus-13-degree cold — one of the most famous games ever, partly BECAUSE of the brutal weather. Exactly the kind of drama a dome makes impossible.
A legendary snowy 2002 playoff game decided by an obscure rule about fumbles — the falling snow is half of what made it unforgettable. Another case of weather becoming a character in the story.
A variable — borrowed from math — is a factor that changes and affects the outcome. Weather has been football’s wildest variable for a century; putting on a roof deletes it from the game.

Competitive equity means fairness of competition — everyone facing the same conditions. A dome team never has to play in snow all season; then a snowy playoff game on the road hits them extra hard. Fair, or just football? That’s the debate.
To neutralize something is to cancel out its power. A snowstorm can neutralize a great passing game — slippery ball, sliding receivers — so a team’s biggest weapon suddenly stops working.

forms: a feature of the sport or merely a bug
text: Borrowed from software: a “feature” is something good that’s there on purpose; a “bug” is a flaw to be fixed. The whole dome debate squeezes into one question — is weather part of what football IS (a feature), or a problem to engineer away (a bug)?

Premium seating is the expensive fancy stuff: private suites (mini rooms with their own snacks), club seats, and loge sections (small roped-off box areas). Roofed stadiums make it easier to sell, because buyers are paying for guaranteed comfort.

Corporate clients are companies — not regular fans — that buy the expensive seats, often to impress their own customers. What they’re really buying is a promise: comfortable, weatherproof, nothing left to chance.

The capital basis is the total money invested in building something. Raise it by $300 million for a roof, and everything inside — tickets, parking, hot dogs — has to cost more to pay it back. As the expert puts it: the roof isn’t free to fans.
The Green Bay Packers’ legendary open-air stadium in Wisconsin, home of freezing “frozen tundra” games since 1957. If any stadium in America will never get a roof, it’s this one.

In pro sports, a franchise is a team — the whole team-as-a-business. Not a fast-food chain. “There will always be franchises” that stay outdoors means some teams’ very identities depend on open-air football.
In business-speak, a market is a city or region where a team sells itself — Green Bay and Buffalo are “markets.” Not a supermarket, and not a farmers market.
Embedded means stuck so deeply inside something that it can’t be pulled out. Outdoor football is embedded in some teams’ identities — take it away and the team wouldn’t feel like the same team.

Untenable means impossible to keep going or defend. Climate change could someday make outdoor football in Miami or Phoenix untenable — simply too dangerously hot. The opposite problem from Buffalo’s snow, same result: a roof.

The two experts the Journal is interviewing: Andrew Zimbalist, an economist famous for studying the business of sports, and Long, a researcher who studies how stadium deals get paid for. The all-caps name at the start of each paragraph tells you whose answer you’re reading.
